children: By Stephen Kreider Yoder and Karen Kreider Yoder
Retirement Rookies

The first few years in retirement are often the most difficult. But they also can set the stage for how you'll fill the years ahead — both financially and psychologically. Stephen Kreider Yoder, 69, a longtime Wall Street Journal editor, joined his wife, Karen Kreider Yoder, 70, in retirement in late 2022. In this monthly Retirement Rookies column, the Yoders chronicle some of the issues they are dealing with early in retirement.
Steve
I am writing these words filled with gratitude.

As Thanksgiving nears, Karen and I have found that retirement is an especially good time to take stock — a rare chance to look back, to appreciate the relationships that endured, the health that still allows us to enjoy our days, and the simple gift of having time that is finally our own.

We are grateful for 5 a.m. on Monday mornings, when one of us brews coffee and plucks the San Francisco Chronicle off the stoop, the other rolls back over to sleep, and neither has a job to break the reverie. It's a daily reminder of just how thankful we are for each other.

We give thanks that we can age in a city that delights us with its row houses, hills, dunes and friends, where caring people urge us to help the unfortunate around us. We are thankful for the road that starts at our front door and sweeps us off on adventures across America.

And we count the blessings that put us here — the privileges we were born into as Americans in loving families, the wide-open career opportunities, the institutions that helped us save for retirement.
Our biggest blessings are the people who got us here. Many of them, I can no longer thank.

I can't thank my expository-writing professor — Mrs. Hartzler, she asked us to call her — a stern master whose glare scared many students. She demanded logic, brevity, grammar and meticulous word choice in a way I found so compelling that I changed my major to English my senior year. She died the year after I graduated, and I see her face every time I edit.
I can't thank Greg, my first boss in the U.S., a curmudgeon who distrusted authority and taught this meek reporter to be tough enough to be his deputy and guided me into my editing career.

I can't thank my late mother, who grew up in a dirt-poor Texas Panhandle farm family and fascinated us with childhood tales. Classmates called her "white trash," she told us with an impish grin, and her first chewing gum was a wad she plucked off a Perryton sidewalk. Her girlhood poverty was a point of pride, and she instilled in me both frugality and the conviction that my potential transcended class.

Fortunately, I can still thank my father, who grew up on a hardscrabble Iowa farm and is still sharp at age 95. In February 1961, he and my mother trundled us children up the gangway onto the SS President Cleveland in San Francisco and shipped off to become career missionaries in Japan — an unimaginable leap of faith to a land still recovering from war.

Their sacrifices in leaving America gave me a wondrous childhood in Northern Japan, where I learned the joys of urban living while straddling cultures. Our family budget was tight, and I concluded that it was my job to find work to fund hobbies and adventures, capitalizing on the independence my parents gave me.
When I flew alone to Indiana for college at age 17, I spoke fluent Japanese.

Eight years later, I was a freelance Japanese-English translator when a tall bearded stranger chanced upon me at a Tokyo lunch table. It was Bradley Martin, bureau chief of The Wall Street Journal's Asian edition. He paid me to interpret at a Ministry of Finance interview — as a lark, he admitted later, to watch the bureaucrats' jaws drop at this American kid's Japanese. He soon gave me a part-time translating gig and, months later, forced me to report a story against my protestations that I had no journalistic talent.
I opened the newspaper, saw my byline, and had my Road to Damascus moment: This was my calling. Over the summer, Brad turned me into a journalist, a career richer than any I could have imagined.

I'm writing here because the sacrifices Dad made cued me up for Brad to take a gamble that guided me into my 38-year career and a life in which hundreds of people helped place me here in a blessed retirement.
Karen
"For the beauty of the earth, for the glory of the skies," we sang around the table at my 70th-birthday dinner last month in Kansas.
It was a hymn of thanks with special poignancy on this birthday. With me were three of my siblings, at the round table where we had gathered so many times with our parents, now long gone.
"For the love which from our birth, over and around us lies," we sang in four-part harmony, "Lord of all to thee we raise, this our hymn of grateful praise."

Steve and I have been singing fragments of that first verse to each other a lot this fall, even more often as Thanksgiving approaches and reminds us of the people in our lives that make our retirement more meaningful.

In San Francisco, that's church friends, former colleagues from schools where I taught, and friends we've made volunteering to develop a new park out by the beach. Retirement gives me more time simply to be with people here.

My 70th-birthday wish list had one entry: Gather with my brother and sisters and share stories. Around the Kansas farmstead table, we ate curry made with bison from a nearby preserve, I blew out a single candle on a birthday flan, and we retreated to the family room.

Each sibling and spouse showed an artifact about me from our past that prompted a story and a question for me — a photo of me in bell-bottoms in college, the first letter Steve wrote to me, before we were dating.

And then their gift of questions. What are your memories of the day we dropped you off for college in South Dakota? Which of your traits do you attribute to Mother? To Dad? As we age, we increasingly express gratitude for the values our parents instilled in us — unconditional love, creativity, an adventuresome spirit, generosity, willingness to let go.
Our three sons, whom we have long since let go, began phoning me that afternoon, giving me their good wishes.
My birthday celebration continued the next morning as we drove west across the Great Plains into the Colorado Rockies with the hymn of gratitude's first stanza in mind, "For the beauty of the earth."

Our retirement has deepened our gratitude for earth's beauty, at home in California, on our travels across America and in Japan. This birthday trip combined gratitude for both earth and family. We drove up an old mining road to the rustic cabin that Dad conceived and we helped build nearly 60 years ago with several other families and that has become a sacred place for our own children.
When we reached the cabin, out popped a birthday surprise: Our eldest son and our daughter-in-law had been lying in wait, bringing me another surge of gratitude.

Our hymn of gratefulness will accompany us again this month as we gaze out the windows of the eastbound Amtrak California Zephyr, absorbing America's beauty as we anticipate Thanksgiving week with our families in the Midwest.

With the tune running in our heads, we will give thanks "For the wonder of each hour, of the day and of the night, hill and vale and tree and flower.... For the joy of human love, brother, sister, parent, child, friends on earth, and friends above."
